title: Stop telling me you're busy
text:
"How are you?" "Busy!" I must have had this conversation a thousand times this year. Everybody, it seems, is busy. My colleagues are busy, my friends are busy, and even my retired neighbour, who spends most of his day in the garden, tells me he is "terribly busy". Somewhere along the way, being busy stopped being a complaint and became a badge of honour.

I understand why. In a culture that values productivity above almost everything else, admitting that you have free time feels dangerous. If you are not busy, people might think you are lazy, unimportant or, worst of all, unsuccessful. So we fill our calendars with meetings, answer emails late at night and proudly tell everyone how exhausted we are.

But is all this activity actually getting us anywhere? I doubt it. Research suggests that after about fifty hours a week, productivity drops so sharply that the extra hours achieve almost nothing. Tired people make more mistakes, forget things and find it harder to come up with new ideas. In other words, the person who stays in the office until nine is often doing the same amount of work as the one who leaves at five – just more slowly and more painfully.

Of course, some people genuinely have too much to do. Parents of young children, people with two jobs and those caring for sick relatives are not busy by choice, and I am not criticising them. My problem is with the rest of us, who choose to be busy because we are afraid of what silence might reveal.

Because that is the uncomfortable truth: being busy is a wonderful excuse. If I am busy, I do not have to call my mother, start that novel I keep talking about, or ask myself whether I actually enjoy my job. Busyness protects us from the big questions.

So here is my suggestion. The next time someone asks how you are, try not to say "busy". Say "fine", or "tired", or "happy", or tell them about something interesting you have done. And once a week, leave an evening completely empty. No plans, no phone, no guilt. You might discover that you are not as busy as you thought – and that your life is more interesting when you have time to notice it.

As for my neighbour, I asked him last week what exactly was keeping him so busy. He thought for a moment and said, "Tomatoes." I have never envied anyone more.
